title: I built a 2-player floor-is-lava tag game with Claude so my sister and I could play on one laptop. Here's what the AI got wrong (and what fixed it)
author: HQBGdotAI
selftext:
I'm not a traditional programmer. I build games by describing them to Claude and testing every version myself. Tagroo started as "tag, but the floor is lava, both of us on one keyboard."



The one design call that made it fun came from me, not the AI: if the runner touches lava the chase ends, but if the chaser falls in they only lose about a second. That asymmetry means the chaser is fighting the map too. Claude's first version punished both equally and it was boring.



Things the AI got wrong that I only caught by playing:



The hazards started ticking during the 3-2-1 countdown, so we'd both spawn into holes and die before the round started. Claude never "saw" it because it was only reading code. Once I described exactly what happened on screen, it was a one-line fix.



If you landed on top of an obstacle you got stuck inside it forever. The fix it came up with was turning that into an automatic vault, which ended up feeling like a feature.



The first art was gray and sad, like a 2005 dungeon. I had to be really specific: bright colors per map, an arena that looks like a lit platform floating in a lava sea. Vague feedback like "make it prettier" got me nowhere.



The lava looked like repeating wallpaper. It took a few rounds of feedback (dark crust plates, glowing veins, two layers at different scales) before it looked like real lava.



Biggest lesson: AI is fast at building, but it can't tell if something is fun. You have to play every build and describe exactly what you see.



It's free in the browser, no sign-up, one keyboard or online with a code: [https://hqbg.ai/tagroo?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=social&utm\_campaign=tagroo](https://hqbg.ai/tagroo?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=tagroo)



Happy to answer questions about the workflow.
